name: Wolfberry (goji)

card.summary: Goji (wolfberry) is a carotenoid- and polysaccharide-rich dried fruit from East Asia that people eat or drink as a longevity food, with claimed benefits for skin, eyes and general vitality.
card.note: Can interact with warfarin; rare allergic reactions reported.

quick.overview:
Goji berries come from the boxthorn species Lycium barbarum and Lycium chinense, grown mainly in Ningxia, China, and used in traditional East Asian medicine for centuries. They are sold dried, as juice, powder or extract.

In health and beauty circles they are eaten for their carotenoids, polysaccharides and polyphenols, with the idea that antioxidants support skin, eyes and healthy ageing. Human trials have looked at antioxidant markers and eye pigment more than at skin appearance.
quick.how: People add dried berries to food and tea, or take juice or powder. It is usually one part of a longevity or antioxidant-rich diet, with effects described as gradual.
quick.risks: Goji is generally eaten as a food, but the literature lists it among herbs that may increase bleeding risk with warfarin, and rare anaphylaxis cases are reported. Pesticide residues have led to regulatory seizures of some imports, and US regulators have warned sellers over unapproved therapeutic claims.

lead: Goji, or wolfberry, is the fruit of Lycium barbarum and Lycium chinense, two boxthorn shrubs in the nightshade family that are native to East Asia and grown mainly in Ningxia, China. The dried red berries have been used in Chinese, Japanese and Korean traditional medicine since at least the 3rd century AD, where the fruit is listed as lycii fructus.[1] The pulp contains carotenoids, polysaccharides (about 30% by one Wikipedia summary), vitamins, fatty acids and a large family of polyphenols.[1][2]

People who eat goji for their looks treat it as an antioxidant and longevity food. The chain they describe runs from carotenoids and polysaccharides, to antioxidant status, to skin that looks healthier and slower visible ageing, with the eyes a traditional focus as well: in Chinese medicine the fruit is described as benefiting the liver, kidney and eyesight.[5] The berries go into porridge, soups, teas and snack mixes, or are taken as juice and powder.[1][15]

Since about 2000 goji has been sold in Western markets as a superfruit, accompanied by a wave of marketing claims, a juice-company class action, and regulatory attention in the UK and US.[1] Human research is made up of small randomised trials: antioxidant enzymes after goji juice, macular pigment after daily berries, a retinitis pigmentosa supplement trial, and a handful of metabolic and dental studies.[3][4][5] Reviews catalogue its polyphenols and its effects on the visual system.[2][13]

angle.text: People eat goji as an antioxidant food in the hope of healthier-looking skin and eyes and slower ageing. A 2021 pilot trial measured skin carotenoids as well as macular pigment after three months of daily berries; no trial has scored skin appearance directly.

paras: Goji refers to the fruit of Lycium barbarum (matrimony vine) and Lycium chinense (Chinese desert-thorn), woody shrubs of the nightshade family, Solanaceae. The two species differ in taste and sugar content. Linnaeus named the genus Lycium in 1753, and the English name goji approximates the Chinese gouqi; the term goji berry has been in use since about 2000.[1]

The Duke of Argyll introduced L. barbarum to Britain in the 1730s, where it was mostly grown for hedging and garden decoration.[1] In Asia the plant has long been cultivated on the Yellow River floodplains of Ningxia. Young shoots and leaves are eaten as a leaf vegetable, and the berries serve as a garnish or sweetener in cooking.[1]

China supplies most of the world's wolfberry products. According to the Wikipedia article, cultivation covered about 325,000 mu (roughly 21,700 hectares) in 2023 and the national wolfberry economy was valued at 29 billion yuan; about 61% of commercially grown Chinese wolfberries come from Ningxia, particularly Zhongning County, with Gansu and Qinghai also growing the crop.[1] Export products include juice concentrate, dried berries, snacks and freeze-dried powder, and North American farmers began commercial cultivation in the 2000s.[1]

Pharmacopoeias list the fruit as lycii fructus and the leaves as herba lycii.[1] A review of Lycium chemistry describes goji as a representative tonic medicine used to nourish the liver and kidney and to benefit essence and eyesight, and notes its use across a wide range of conditions in traditional Chinese medicine.[5]

Cooks add the dried berries to porridge, soups, teas and snack mixes. Posters on the strength-training forum T Nation mention goji in oat porridge, breakfast compotes and meal-prep bowls, which illustrates how it appears in ordinary diet logs of people who train.[15][16]

The berries are consumed for their antioxidants, with the aim of supporting skin and eyes and general vitality. Reviews of antioxidants and vascular health discuss how reactive oxygen species contribute to tissue damage, which is the basis for interest in antioxidant foods generally.[7] Wolfberry polyphenols were reported to show radical-scavenging activity in laboratory assays.[2]

The dried fruit is also a source of zeaxanthin, a carotenoid. Carotenoid intake is measured in skin by optical methods in some studies, and a 2021 pilot trial using that measurement is described below.[4] Animal work on UVB skin damage exists, but human trials of goji have not scored skin appearance.[14]

Goji contains polysaccharides (the Lycium barbarum polysaccharides, or LBP), carotenoids, vitamins, fatty acids, peptidoglycans and polyphenols.[1] A phytochemical study isolated nine new phenylpropanoids, one new coumarin and 43 known polyphenols from wolfberry, bringing the total identified to 53, and reported that all showed oxygen-radical absorbance capacity in laboratory tests.[2] A 2024 review of phenolamides proposes these compounds as markers for quality evaluation across Lycium species.[6]

LBP is the component most studied for the eye. A review of the visual system describes antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anti-excitotoxic and anti-apoptotic properties of LBP, with most work focused on the retina, including models of glaucoma, ischemia, age-related macular degeneration, retinitis pigmentosa and diabetic retinopathy.[13]

From about 2000, dried berries, juice and powders became popular in developed countries as snacks and alternative-medicine products, often with exaggerated health claims.[1] In 2003 a booklet by Earl Mindell, Goji: The Himalayan Health Secret, made anti-cancer claims and popularised a story of a herbalist named Li Qing Yuen who supposedly lived from 1677 to 1933; the Wikipedia article describes the story as unsupported.[1]

In January 2007 a CBC Marketplace investigation covered a goji juice product; the article reports that Mindell, then working for the company FreeLife, had said Memorial Sloan-Kettering research showed wolfberry juice would prevent 75% of breast cancers, a claim described there as false.[1] A class action was filed in US District Court in Arizona on 29 May 2009 against FreeLife over its Himalayan Goji Juice, GoChi and TaiSlim products, and a settlement on 28 April 2010 required the company to stop marketing the products as unheated or raw.[1]

Marketing of berries as organic Himalayan produce has also been questioned: the Wikipedia article notes that farming on the Tibetan Plateau, where many Himalayan berries are said to originate, is conventional.[1]

A 30-day randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of 50 healthy Chinese adults aged 55 to 72 gave 120 mL daily of an LBP-standardised juice (GoChi) or placebo. Serum superoxide dismutase rose 8.4% and glutathione peroxidase 9.9%, and malondialdehyde fell 8.7%, with significant differences from placebo at the end; the study was published in 2009 by researchers linked to the product's maker.[3]

A randomised, unmasked pilot trial of 27 adults aged 45 to 65 compared 28 g of goji berries five days a week with a lutein-zeaxanthin supplement for 90 days. Macular pigment optical density rose at two retinal eccentricities in the goji group (p = 0.029 and 0.044) but not in the supplement group, and skin carotenoids rose at day 45 and day 90 in the goji group only.[4]

In a double-masked, placebo-controlled 12-month trial in retinitis pigmentosa, 42 participants completed the study (23 on Lycium barbarum granules, 19 on placebo). The authors reported no deterioration of visual acuity in the treatment group relative to placebo and less thinning of the macular layer, while visual-field sensitivity and electroretinogram differences were not significant.[5]

Other randomised trials include a 16-week study of 24 middle-aged and older adults following a healthy dietary pattern with or without 15 g of wolfberry daily, in which the dietary pattern improved blood outgrowth endothelial cell function and the added wolfberry produced no further effect;[10] a 3-month trial of 67 people with type 2 diabetes in which LBP lowered serum glucose and raised HDL;[11] and a trial of goji mouthwash alongside scaling and root planing in periodontitis.[12] A monograph summary reports that three or more months of intake may improve cardiometabolic risk factors in healthy Chinese adults, graded as low-quality evidence.[1] Reviews summarise effects on the visual system.[13] No trial has used a skin-appearance outcome.

A systematic review of 149 articles on warfarin interactions lists Chinese wolfberry among the foods and herbs for which clinicians should be aware of increased bleeding risk, and advises patients to consult healthcare professionals before starting new herbs or supplements.[8] Laboratory tests suggest goji tea compounds may inhibit cytochrome P450 enzymes involved in drug metabolism.[1] Goji has also been reported among rare triggers of anaphylaxis, and people sensitive to other nightshade plants are noted as a possible risk group.[9][14]

The FDA has detected insecticide and fungicide residues in some Chinese-origin imports, and its Import Alert 9908 has led to seizures; Grokipedia additionally mentions heavy-metal and sulfite findings in some retail samples.[1][14] In the UK, the Food Standards Agency removed goji from its Novel Foods list on 18 June 2007 on the basis of a history of consumption before 1997.[1] In the US, the FDA sent warning letters on 6 August 2019 and 23 July 2020 to sellers whose therapeutic claims it said made products unapproved new drugs.[1]

Goji is often listed with other tonic and longevity foods used in East Asian diets, including red dates and ginseng in soups and teas, and with Western superfruits such as acai and bee pollen.[14][15] The carotenoid zeaxanthin links it to dietary approaches centred on lutein and zeaxanthin for the eyes, which the 2021 trial compared directly.[4]

lore.intro: In fitness and looksmaxxing communities goji turns up mostly as a food ingredient in porridge, smoothie bowls and diet logs, or as a stock longevity item in lists of antioxidant foods.[15][16] Strong claims about it come chiefly from supplement marketing rather than from forum users.

claims.claim: Goji berries are an antioxidant food that supports healthier-looking skin
claims.believers: Proponents point to goji's carotenoids, polysaccharides and polyphenols and to its long use as a tonic in East Asia, and say antioxidant foods support skin and healthy ageing.[5]
claims.experts: Laboratory work shows radical-scavenging activity for wolfberry polyphenols,[2] and a pilot trial measured raised skin carotenoids after 90 days of daily berries;[4] no trial has scored skin appearance.

claims.claim: Goji raises the body's own antioxidant enzymes
claims.believers: Juice marketers cite a trial in which serum antioxidant enzymes increased over 30 days.[3]
claims.experts: The 30-day study of 50 healthy older adults found SOD and GSH-Px up about 8 to 10% versus placebo, in a product-maker-linked study; its authors suggest longer use may matter.[3]

claims.believers: Traditional medicine describes goji as brightening the eyesight, and supplement sellers cite zeaxanthin content.[5]
claims.experts: A 90-day pilot trial found increased macular pigment optical density with berries but not with a lutein-zeaxanthin supplement; a 12-month retinitis pigmentosa trial reported less macular thinning than placebo.[4][5]

claims.claim: Goji berries from the Himalayas are a rare, organic superfood
claims.believers: Early 2000s marketing described unheated Himalayan berries with unique benefits, a story promoted in Mindell's 2003 booklet.[1]
claims.experts: The Wikipedia article reports that a 2010 settlement limited raw marketing and that farming on the Tibetan Plateau is conventional; the FDA has found pesticide residues in some imports.[1]

claims.claim: Goji juice prevents or treats cancer
claims.believers: Seller claims in the 2000s cited cancer outcomes, including a claimed Memorial Sloan-Kettering finding.[1]
claims.experts: The Wikipedia article describes the Memorial Sloan-Kettering claim as false, and the FDA sent warning letters in 2019 and 2020 over therapeutic claims.[1]

claims.claim: Goji is harmless because it is just a fruit
claims.believers: Users treat it as a food, eaten daily in porridge and snacks.[15][16]
claims.experts: A systematic review lists Chinese wolfberry among herbs that may raise bleeding risk on warfarin, and rare anaphylaxis is reported.[8][9]
